paper_title: Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: World models have made rapid progress in simulating the physical side of world (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2025; Brooks et al., 2024): given past observations and control signals, they predict how scenes evolve (Bruce et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2023; NVIDIA, 2025), with increasingly realistic dynamics, appearance, and long-range consistency (Google DeepMind, 2024; Parker-Holder & Fruchter, 2025; Robbyant Team, 2026; Gao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026a). In most of these works, however, intelligence resides outside the world. user steers the generated world through inputs with limited degrees of freedom, such as keyboard and mouse commands, gamepad actions, or text prompts, but nothing within the world perceives the full state of the user in real time or decides how to respond. Such worlds can be accurate, yet they remain lifeless: there is world to explore, but no one to talk to. We argue that intelligence and physical reality are equally fundamental to world. Building on this view, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM). The RWM generates world inhabited by living presences and connects it to the real world through full-duplex, real-time interaction. Each side continuously perceives audio and video from the other and can respond, interrupt, or remain silent while the other is still acting. This reciprocal interaction requires two complementary capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audiovisual behavior. These functional roles can be fulfilled by unified multimodal model or by modular system combining multimodal language model with diffusion model. In this report, we present Duo v1, modular instantiation of the RWM. Interaction proceeds in chunks of 17 video frames, approximately 0.71 at 24 fps. Three technical designs coordinate Intent and Realization within single streaming system. In most audio-visual video generative model (MiniMax, 2026), Autoregressive intent for interaction. language model serves as an instruction encoder for the diffusion model. In Duo v1, the intent module instead reasons over the ongoing interaction autoregressively and makes participation decisions: at every chunk, it emits <speak> action followed by text or <wait> action, conditioned on the user input so far and its own earlier language. Its hidden states, rather than its decoded text alone, carry each decision to the realization module (Sec. 3). Action-aware rebalancing prevents the intent module from collapsing into perpetual waiting, since most chunks contain no new assistant speech, and history perturbations teach it to recover from imperfect earlier responses (Sec. 4). Causal chunk conditions on unified timeline. User speech, user video, intent tokens, and assistant media are synchronized on one timeline, and each chunk is given exactly the conditions that are available at its decision boundary. Module-specific attention masks enforce causality within and across chunks. In the intent module, temporal patches are completed inside each chunk, so no future frame leaks into decision through the visual frontend. In the realization module, noisy media tokens of chunk can attend to the reference, intent features, and clean history, but not to their own clean targets or to any later chunk (Sec. 3). Dual rollout distillation. Before distillation, the realization module is trained on intent features of recorded assistant text and on recorded media history, whereas in live exchange both are produced by the system itself. Dual rollout brings inference-time conditioning into distillation: within each training window, the frozen Intent Module autoregressively generates the final assistant turn, and the Realization Module conditions on the resulting intent features and its own generated audiovisual history. Distribution matching distillation on these rollouts yields four-step streaming generator trained under conditions that match live interaction. We develop several data construction pipelines and streaming runtime to support Duo v1. The training data combine scripted synthetic video calls and recorded conversations, with audio, video, and text aligned on shared timeline for causal interaction training (Sec. 5). The streaming pipeline coordinates intent inference, audiovisual generation, and incremental decoding while continuing to capture user inputs (Sec. 6). Speech and vision provide rich, direct channel between the two worlds, conveying information that keyboard and mouse commands often fail to capture, including tone, timing, expression, and visual details of real objects, actions, and scenes. This richer interface creates opportunities for wide range of shared activities shaped jointly by real and generated participants.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: World models and persistent interaction. World Models and Dreamer learn predictive representations for control (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2025), while Genie learns action-controllable environments from video (Bruce et al., 2024). LingBot-World studies data engine and staged causal adaptation for 3 continuing visual worlds (Robbyant Team, 2026). These works connect learned dynamics to an agents actions and subsequent observations. Full-duplex and multimodal participation. Moshi represents concurrent user and assistant speech streams (Defossez et al., 2024). Qwen-Omni separates multimodal understanding from streaming speech generation through connected Thinker and Talker components (Xu et al., 2025a;b). Wan-Streamer extends the streaming setting to audiovisual foundation models and their execution schedule (Huang et al., 2026b). ELLSA jointly models full-duplex speech, gesture, and expression, including non-verbal behavior while listening (Wang et al., 2026). These works establish participation timing and visible communicative behavior as closely related modeling problems. Joint and streaming audiovisual generation. Ovi, MOVA, and LTX develop synchronized audiovisual generation through coupled modality streams (Low et al., 2025; SII-OpenMOSS Team, 2026; HaCohen et al., 2026). MiniMax-H3 is reference-conditioned audiovisual generator whose weights can initialize related models (MiniMax, 2026). Audio-driven animation methods such as EMO and OmniHuman realize visible behavior from supplied speech (Tian et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025). LiveTalk combines distilled video performer with streaming audio from Qwen-Omni (Chern et al., 2025). These approaches connect speech with visible articulation and motion, with different choices of conditioning and generation order. Streaming joint diffusion further requires audio and video to remain aligned as their generated histories grow. OmniForcing addresses this conversion through asymmetric block-causal alignment, audio-sink stabilization, and joint self-generated rollouts (Su et al., 2026). OmniLiveAvatar combines progressive autoregressive distillation, synchronized audio-video memory, and rolling prompt planning (Zhu et al., 2026b). Causal adaptation and few-step training. Diffusion Forcing assigns different noise levels across sequence, and CausVid distills bidirectional generator into causal few-step student (Chen et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2025). Self Forcing uses self-generated history during training to reduce the context mismatch with autoregressive inference (Huang et al., 2025). Work on causal-compatible initialization further aligns teacher and student during the transition to few-step generation (Zhu et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026). Consistency models and distribution matching provide complementary tools for reducing sampling steps (Song et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2024b), with later distribution-matching work incorporating multistep alignment and adversarial training (Yin et al., 2024a).

sections.title: 3 Architecture
sections.content: Duo v1 couples language-based Intent Module with causal audiovisual Realization Module  (Fig. 2)  . Hidden states produced by the Intent Module serve as the interface between the two modules, providing semantic guidance for the joint generation of video and stereo audio for the assistant. The two modules process complementary inputs and maintain separate histories, integrating response planning and audiovisual synthesis within unified architecture. The following subsections describe this design in detail: Sec. 3.1 formalizes the interaction between the two modules, Sec. 3.2 details the Intent Module, Sec. 3.3 describes the audio-visual latent space, and Sec. 3.4 presents the causal joint generator used by the Realization Module. 3.1 The Overview of Reciprocal World Model RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental components of world. Their interaction is reciprocal: Intent determines how the system responds to the evolving environment, while Realization expresses that intent through audiovisual behavior, which in turn becomes part of the environment for subsequent interaction. We formalize this process as chunk-wise, full-duplex interaction. Let hk denote the hidden states produced by the Intent Module for this output, and zk = (zv ) the latent representations of the generated video and audio. The Intent Module adapts a pretrained multimodal language backbone (Bai et al., 2025) to causal, chunk-wise

Video frames and audio samples are mapped to the same half-open chunk intervals using source timestamps. Assistant text targets are assigned to chunks according to speech onset, while the initial chunk uses fixed <wait> action  (Fig. 3)  . sections.title: 4 Training Strategy
sections.content: Training proceeds in three stages. Stage 1 trains the Intent Module for causal participation and text prediction through supervised fine-tuning. Stage 2 trains the Realization Module for causal joint audiovisual generation, conditioned on recorded media history and intent features extracted from recorded assistant text by the frozen Intent Module  (Fig. 4)  . Stage 3 distills four-step generation through distribution matching, with dual rollout using predicted text and generated audiovisual history to match inference-time conditioning. 4.1 Stage 1: Intent Training We adapt the multimodal Intent Module with causal supervised fine-tuning on chunk-aligned conversations. At the start of chunk k, the model predicts the assistant output text yk from the global instruction d, the user video uv and ASR text ut available through chunk 1, and earlier assistant language y<k. The decision context excludes assistant video. In the training data, user tokens become available at the ends of their aligned spans, while assistant text tokens are assigned to the chunk containing their speech onset. The <speak> action introduces new text, including continuations of an earlier turn. The <wait> action adds no new text and can coexist with ongoing playback or non-verbal behavior. Fig. 3 illustrates this shift, and Sec. 3.2 details the input protocol. Causal chunk supervision. Let yk be the token sequence of the assistant output in chunk k, and let CI = (d, uv,<k, ut,<k, y<k) denote the causal context of the Intent Module. We minimize the weighted autoregressive objective intent = k,j mk,jwk,j log pϕ (cid:16) 1, max (cid:16) yk,j k,j mk,jwk,j CI k, yk,<j (cid:17) (cid:17) , (5) where yk,j is the j-th action, content, or structural token, wk,j is its category-dependent weight, and mk,j is one for supervised tokens and zero otherwise. The denominator sums the effective weights within each sampled conversation, with minimum of one. The initial assistant output y0 is fixed <wait> used as context and excluded from the loss. Action-aware rebalancing. Most chunks introduce no new assistant text, so unweighted training can favor waiting. We assign supervision categories offline from recorded assistant events and from whether the user is speaking at the chunk start. This speaking status distinguishes idle waits from waits during user speech and ordinary openings from interruption openings. The assistant annotation distinguishes openings from continuations, and an annotated question in the preceding user turn provides separate opening tag. We use these labels to subsample targets and weight the loss, with separate action and content weights and adjustments for opening categories. Subsampled targets remain in the conversation history. The model receives only the causal context described above. Validation retains the full set of eligible targets and reports separate token-level metrics for actions, speech, and waits. Training under imperfect assistant history. To expose the model to imperfect histories, we truncate or repeat text in selected continuation chunks, mask their losses, and retain supervision on later valid targets. For missed-opening recovery, we replace selected ordinary openings with <wait> in the history and mask their losses. In the next chunk of the same assistant turn, only <speak> contributes to the loss. Preserving visual and linguistic grounding. The training mixture contains examples whose correct answer depends on the user video as well as examples solvable from text alone. We identify visually grounded assistant turns through data inspection and upweight their content-token loss, while retaining the same causal visual input path. Prompt augmentation varies the format, ordering, and completeness of the static 8 Figure 4: Overview of Stage 1 (Intent Training) and Stage 2 (Realization Training). assistant/scene description without inventing new facts. Together with source-grouped train/validation splits, these choices discourage the Intent Module from relying on fixed prompt template or on text-only shortcuts. Optional emotion labels are kept as separately weighted attachments and are admitted only at their annotated causal boundary. We use low-rank adaptation to fine-tune the Intent Module. After this stage, the frozen Intent Module supplies hidden states from its forward passes to condition media training. 4.2 Stage 2: Realization Training Stage 2 trains the Realization Module for causal joint audiovisual generation while keeping the Intent Module frozen. sections.title: 5 Data Construction
sections.content: Training Duo v1 requires temporally aligned user inputs and assistant audiovisual behavior. We combine synthetic and recorded interactions into unified conversation timeline, preserving natural timing and controlled events. This provides causal supervision for Intent and audiovisual targets for Realization, with additional routes for missing-view reconstruction and recorded-video extensions.

sections.title:
5.1 Synthetic Data
Pipeline overview. This route generates a two-person video call in which both participants are rendered
together. Fig. 7 shows its two stages. Stage I is text only. Control cards are sampled, a LLM writes a structured
screenplay under these cards, rule checks reject invalid screenplays, and a template converts each screenplay
block into a text prompt (MiniMax, 2026). Stage II feeds these prompts to a t2v model, which generates
one split-screen audio-video stream block by block. The left panel is always the user and the right panel
the assistant. Generating both panels and the shared audio on a unified timeline preserves the timing of
dialogue, reactions, overlaps, and interruptions.
sections.content: Control cards. Without explicit constraints, LLM-generated conversations tend to repeat similar topics, relationships, and turn-taking patterns. To improve diversity, we use control cards that define attributes with predefined candidate values. For each screenplay, these values are sampled uniformly and included as explicit requirements in the generation prompt. duration: language: persona: 30 s, 45 s, 60 { Chinese, English { } , e.g., relationship none, relationship, occupation } { patient, . . . micro-actions: (12 values), occupation { } } firefighter, nurse, chef, . . . { , where on suggests 24 small reactions, e.g., } { off, on { away briefly, . . . parent-child, colleagues, doctor- (11 values, per participant) nod, raise an eyebrow, look } interaction: emotion: fixed to follow the topic and the conversation resolution: everyday exchange, interruption, follow-up / debate, proactive inquiry { 576, 1536 768 } , used only by video synthesis } { } Each interaction value carries written specification. For example, interruption requires one speaker to cut in before the other finishes, brief overlap of voices, and the interrupted speaker yielding the turn. Screenplay and t2v prompt synthesis. The sampled cards are inserted into fixed template, and the LLM writes synopsis followed by JSON screenplay, shown in Fig. 8 (a). The screenplay describes each participant once (appearance, voice, environment, initial pose) and then splits the call into blocks of 515 at natural turn boundaries. Each block is an ordered list of events. An event pairs description of expressions, gestures, and the listeners reaction with at most one speech entry, so nonverbal reactions need no invented dialogue. rule-based validator checks the structure, block timing, language, and the absence of capture-device words such as phone in the narration, and returns errors to the LLM for up to 3 attempts. The validated screenplay is converted into one t2v prompt per block by template, without further LLM calls (Fig. 8(b)). Screenplay fields fill the slots verbatim. The shaded sentences are fixed for all samples and fall into three groups: Reference roles. Each input is assigned one job: the previous final frame is the starting state, the opening video only sets picture quality, and the opening audio only sets voices and room tone. Without these roles the model tends to replay the reference video or repeat its dialogue. Picture content. Each panel is the participants own front camera, which rules out third-person, mirror, and behind-the-back views. Recording devices, UI elements, and subtitles, which otherwise appear frequently in generated calls, are excluded, and content may not cross the center divider, so the two crops stay clean. Causal order. reaction may start only after its trigger has finished, so the assistant view never responds before the user acts. Video synthesis. As shown in Fig. 7, Block 0 receives its prompt and white layout image whose two panels are separated by thin black divider. The layout image fixes only the split-screen geometry, and the model creates both participants and backgrounds from the prompt. Previous final frame (orange). The last frame of block 1 is temporally aligned with the first target frame, preserving pose, expression, and framing across blocks. 13 Figure 7: Screenplay-driven dual-view generation. Stage turns sampled control cards into validated structured screenplay and renders it, without another LLM call, into one t2v prompt per block. Stage II generates one split-screen audio-video block by block. Each later block starts from the previous blocks final frame (orange) and is anchored to the same opening segment of block 0 (blue), so identity and voice references are never re-chained through earlier continuations. Frames and dialogue in this figure come from one generated 30 sample. Opening video (blue). The first 124 frames of block 0 serve as picture-quality reference for brightness, exposure, color sharpness, and noise. Opening audio (blue). The full block 0 audio anchors both voices and room tone. We preserve generation conditions in their original representations, using VAE latents for the initial video and raw RGB for the final frame. The generated video are then concatenated and split into user and assistant views, both sharing the same synchronized audio track. Error accumulation. The baseline data synthesis method conditions each block on the final frame of the preceding block, causing visual errors to accumulate over time. Our synthesis method mitigates this drift by using the opening video (block 0) as fixed reference throughout generation. Fig. 9 compares the two synthesis strategies over 60 sequence of ten 6 blocks. The baseline loses 34.2 luma levels by block 9, with increasingly exaggerated facial textures. Our method stabilizes at approximately 99 luma after slight initial decline, maintaining consistent facial appearance through block 9. 5.2 Recorded Data As shown in Fig. 10, we organize recorded data into six categories by source and interaction format: singlestream video, synchronous dual-stream video, asynchronous dual-stream video, live streams with audience comments, duplex audio recordings and open datasets. The following common recording standards apply across these categories. Recordings feature real speakers and their original voices, with speaker identities, transcripts, and temporal mappings retained and unrelated audio excluded. For video data, each delivered clip preserves continuous, uncut half-body or full-body view with accurate audiovisual synchronization, 14 Figure 8: Screenplay and t2v prompt. (a) The screenplay written by the LLM for the sample in Fig. 7. (b) The t2v prompt rendered from it for continuation block. Shaded sentences are fixed text shared by all samples, grouped as [1]-[3] in the main text. marks screenplay fields copied into the prompt, and the remaining lines are abridged template text. at least 720p effective resolution per view, and no visual overlays. Dual-stream recordings contain at least one complete conversational exchange. Single-stream video. Fig. 10 (b) illustrates single-stream recordings, such as solo podcasts and single-person presentations. The clips range from 10 to 90 seconds, preserving natural pauses. Synchronous dual-stream video. Synchronous dual-stream video, illustrated in Fig. 10 (c), keeps both participants visible at the same time and preserves listening behavior, overlapping speech, and reactions. Asynchronous dual-stream video. Asynchronous dual-stream video shows participants in separate clips that alternate with the speaking turns, as in the interview footage shown in Fig. 10 (d). Live streams with audience comments. We align timestamped audience questions with presenter responses and reconstruct user videos, converting live streams into synchronized dual-stream conversations. Duplex audio recordings. This category consists of full-duplex audio recordings of two-person dialogues, which drive the further video synthesis, as illustrated in Fig. 10 (f). Open datasets. We collected single-stream talking videos from open-source datasets. As depicted in Fig. 10 (g), we filtered the material according to the common recording standards (e.g., resolution require15 Figure 9: Error accumulation over 60 s, ten-block rollout. Top: mean luma (0255) of the full split-screen frame per block (table) and per frame (plot). Bottom: the split-screen frame at the middle of blocks 0, 3, 6, and 9. Base conditions each block only on the previous final frame, and Ours adds the fixed block-0 picture-quality reference. Both runs share the same block 0 and screenplay. ments) and then applied face detection, video understanding, voice activity detection (VAD), automatic speech recognition (ASR), and language identification to guide further filtering and annotation. 5.3 Data Processing 5.3.1 Synthetic Data Quality Control Each newly generated video segment undergoes four automatic quality checks. First-frame consistency. We compare the first frame with the conditioning image, requiring an SSIM of at least 0.90 and perceptual-hash Hamming distance of at most 4. Conditioning uses the character image initially, then the preceding segments processed final frame. Unexpected audio. We compare the generated audio with the source audio using loudness normalization, waveform residuals, and VAD, rejecting segments with unexplained audio activity lasting at least 0.40 s. Camera push-in. We track face scale at 4 FPS, using the first valid detection as the baseline. Rejection thresholds for sustained and abrupt enlargement are smoothed scale of 1.30 times baseline for 0.75 and 1.22-fold jump within 0.50 s, respectively. Persistent large-area visual changes. We sample frames at 4 FPS and measure LAB differences, changedpixel proportions, and color/brightness histogram distances. Using these metrics, we reject abrupt changes that remain above thresholds relative to the pre-change frame, or cumulative drift from the initial frame exceeding both appearance and histogram thresholds. 5.3.2 Live-Stream Data Processing Collection and initial screening. We collect archived live streams and deduplicate source records. Sampled frames are used to check the presence of real participants and visual quality, retaining only suitable material. 16 Figure 10: Recorded data sources, interaction formats The six categories describe the recorded sources, with selected categories requiring further processing or synthesis to construct training examples. Annotation and filtering. We produce transcripts with wordor character-level timestamps by Qwen3ASR-1.7B and Qwen3-ForcedAligner-0.6B (Shi et al., 2026). And we also use Silero VAD (Silero Team, 2024) to identify speech and silence intervals and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B (Xu et al., 2025a) to review audio types. Speaker diarization and speaker-count checks combine FSMN-VAD (Gao et al., 2023) for speech detection, Paraformer (Gao et al., 2022)for transcription, and CAM++ (Wang et al., 2023) for speaker embeddings followed by clustering. These checks exclude windows containing singing, whispered or breathy speech, or multiple speakers, producing timestamped candidate material for dialogue construction. Dialogue construction and video preparation. To obtain the content and timing needed for user-side video synthesis, we match audience comments extracted from real chat logs to the presenters responses. 17 When such matching is not possible, we will generate counterpart utterances and schedule their interjections based on the presenters original speech and available silence. After reviewing conversational coherence, completeness, and audio-visual correspondence, we extract continuous assistant-side video segments and crop them around the presenter to remove on-screen comments and watermarks. We then synthesize the corresponding user-side videos and pair the two views on shared timeline. After final quality check, we deliver clean dual-stream videos together with their transcripts, dialogue timing and source metadata.

sections.title: 6 Streaming Pipeline and Acceleration
sections.content: In this section, we detail our streaming inference design. The system employs an orchestrated scheduling strategy to synchronize the intent module, the realization module and the VAE decoding, ensuring lowlatency performance for interactive tasks.

sections.title:
6.1 Orchestrated Streaming Pipeline
The front-end device continuously captures user audio and video and forwards them for chunk-wise
processing. As shown in Fig. 11, each chunk passes through input acquisition, intent inference, joint
latent generation, and streaming decoding, while input capture continues during response generation. The
sequential stages of the pipeline can be summarized as:
sections.content: Interaction sampling. At 24 frames per second, each sampling window contains 17 video frames and the corresponding user audio, matching the video VAE grouping described in Sec. 3.3. The window duration is tsample = 17/24 708 ms. Intent inference. The Intent Module processes the available context, generates participation and text output, and provides hidden states to the Realization Module. Depending on the input and context length, inference takes tintent = 90160 ms. Joint latent generation. Conditioned on the intent representation and media context, the Realization 576 resolution, this stage Module jointly generates audio and video latents. For video generation at 768 takes tgen = 200-450 ms, depending on the context length. Streaming decoding. The generated audio and video latents are decoded incrementally for playback. Decoding 4-frame group takes approximately tdecode = 30 ms. Other overhead. Data movement, transmission to the front-end device, and display processing contribute approximately toverhead = 40 ms. The reported intent inference, latent generation, and overhead terms sum to tintent + tgen + toverhead 330650 ms. (15) The delay to the first visible output additionally includes the initial decoding time and any remaining wait for the sampling window to close. An utterance or action ending within sampling window can incur an additional sampling delay of up to approximately 708 ms. During playback, we post-process the generated frames to maintain visual stability and smooth motion. 6.2 Causal Latent Decoding The original VAE in (MiniMax, 2026) decodes 5 latent frames into 17 video frames and requires 2 latent frames of lookahead. This dependency introduces additional waiting at chunk boundaries during streaming playback. We therefore adapt the decoding procedure to process available video latents incrementally. After joint generation of response chunk, its video latents are decoded one at time. Each latent produces four video frames, followed by temporal alignment to match the original playback schedule and preserve the 17-frame chunk duration. This procedure allows playback to begin from the available chunk without waiting for additional latents from the next chunk. At 24 frames per second, the shortest playback interval corresponds to the first latent in each group, which represents one video frame after temporal alignment. This interval is 1/24 41.7 ms. The measured per-latent decoding time is approximately 30 ms, below this interval. The decoder can therefore keep pace with playback provided that generated latents are available on schedule. 6.3 Inference Acceleration The runtime coordinates memory management, stage scheduling, and GPU placement to sustain continuous audiovisual generation. Each input chunk covers 17/24 of captured audio and video. Sustained playback 18 Figure 11: Streaming inference on eight GPUs. Time advances from left to right. As shown in Fig. 11, the system runs on single server with eight GPUs. For each response chunk, Intent Module inference precedes joint audiovisual latent generation by the DiT. The remaining VAE decoding steps for one chunk overlap with Intent Module inference for the following chunk, reducing the interval between successive outputs. After restart, the manager reconstructs the active media cache by replaying completed latents through clean forwards in their original order, following the same reset boundaries and retention policy. sections.title: 7 Evaluation and Showcase
sections.content: 7.1 Human Evaluation Evaluation protocol We evaluated the model on 30 real-time duplex interaction cases, each pairing users audio-visual input with the models generated audio-visual reply, replayed side by side on shared timeline. Each reply is judged the way an end user would experience it, at normal playback speed with sound, against six binary criteria: content responsiveness, language adherence, speech intelligibility, visual identity stability, audio-visual synchronization, and audio-visual emotional consistency. Every criterion has written failure conditions, and no partial credit is given. Results Of 180 checks (30 cases 6 criteria), 168 passed (93.3%). The clearest strength is generation fidelity: the model passed all 90 checks on language adherence, speech intelligibility, and visual identity stability. Every reply came in the expected language as complete, intelligible speech, and no case showed visible identity swap, facial or body malformation, or unexplained change in appearance. Cross-modal coherence is nearly as strong. Vocal emotion was consistent with facial expression and body language in 96.7% of cases, and lip movement stayed aligned with speech in 90.0%. Where headroom remains Content responsiveness, which asks whether reply substantively addresses what the user has just said and shown, reached 73.3% (22/30). It is the most demanding criterion in the protocol, since duplex model must settle on reply while speech and video are still streaming in. The misses fall mainly into two patterns. The first is the long tail of conversation, such as jokes and odd remarks, where fitting reply requires reading intent beyond the literal words, and doing so in real time. The second is intent that only becomes clear when speech and video are read together. In one case, user sitting indoors said they had just unlocked shared bike when it started to rain. Given the indoor setting, this reads as complaint, yet the model treated it as request for advice and suggested holding off on riding. Both patterns come down to inferring what the user means from everything they say and show, at conversational speed. This is one of the hardest problems in duplex interaction and the central focus of our next iteration, which builds on foundation that already passed every language, speech, and identity check. 7.2 Showcase Fig. 12 organizes selected examples: plan revision, visual guidance, collaborative design, social support, and interactive customization. These categories connect language to change in shared plan, an observable action, joint solution, or an affective response. The first four categories use script-conditioned training data, the customization example comes from the user demonstration. Fig. 13 extends the coverage to negotiation, decision support, explanation, and task coordination. Fig. 14 adds collaborative creation, coaching, shared experience, turn negotiation, and supportive responses.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced the Reciprocal World Model and its initial implementation, Duo v1, which couples multimodal Intent Module with causal audiovisual Realization Module. This report describes the architecture, training procedure, and runtime scheduling used to generate responses while continuing to receive user input. Duo v1 remains preliminary and currently supports basic audiovisual conversation. The examples illustrate this functionality, while response timing, consistency over longer sessions, and recovery from misunderstandings still require broader evaluation. Development is ongoing, and an updated version will follow soon. 21 Figure 12: Five functions of userassistant interaction. Examples connect dialogue to plans, visible actions, shared solutions, social responses, and interactive customization. Panels (a)-(d) show offline, script-conditioned paired-video data. Panel (e) shows successive moments from provided project demo. 22 Figure 13: Decisions and coordination. Six additional script-conditioned paired-video examples illustrate how the user and assistant question proposal, revise plan, reason through constraints, explain visible evidence, and coordinate shared task. Figure 14: Grounded and social responses. Seven additional script-conditioned conversations connect visible context and dialogue to creative, instructional, and supportive behavior. Panels (a)-(f) show different conversations. Panel (g) shows two moments from one conversation.
